newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.Korean naphtha buyers to honour Itochu trades.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean naphtha buyers to honour Itochu trades.

text.p: South Korean petrochemical companies will honour all existing naphtha contracts with Itochu Corp despite their concerted action to temporarily suspend trade with the Japanese trading house, industry sources said on Friday.
Amid allegations of manipulating prices, seven South Korean petrochemical companies declared on Wednesday they would stop trading open-spec naphtha with Itochu until April arrival cargoes.
But the decision only applies to possible future deals and all existing open positions with Itochu would be honoured, said a South Korean petrochemical trader.
He said most open deals involved deliveries for December and January.
The suspension was just between private enterprises with no involvement by regulatory authorities, he said.
"It applies for trade until three months from now. After that we can change our mind if they (Itochu) change," the trader said.
A source at South Korea's Yukong Ltd told Reuters the country's largest refiner will follow the petrochemical's action against Itochu if they were to ask the refiners to join in.
Yukong plans to shut down a 15,000 barrel-per-day reformer indefinitely from Monday due to the high costs of its naphtha feedstock.
South Korean traders said with their current action, they hoped to see naphtha prices consolidate until they reach their proper spread to crude.

The differential or "crack" between Brent and Tokyo's foward open-specification (open-spec) contract was usually $50 to $60 dollars a tonne. Since the begining of the week, the crack for Febraury Brent/first-half Febraury open-spec had weakened from $76 to just below $70, traders said on late Friday.
But sources in Japan said on Friday, Itochu still appeared to be an active buyer of the open-spec.

They said the impact of the dispute on the market was minimal as Itochu is only the third or fourth biggest supplier into the South Korean market with exports of around 500,000 tonnes per year (12,000-bpd).
Open-spec levels on Friday rebounded with crude with second-half February assessed at $229.00/$231.00 a tonne from Thursday's $226.00/$228.00.
